entities.name: Byzantine Empire under the Isaurian dynasty
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Byzantine Empire under the Isaurian dynasty (717-802 CE), founded when Leo III repelled a massive Arab siege of Constantinople (717-718 CE) that threatened to extinguish the empire, was primarily defined by the Iconoclasm controversy — the emperor's controversial decree banning religious images (icons) that split the Byzantine Church, alienated Rome, and triggered civil war within the empire. The Arab siege failure (718 CE) was arguably the most consequential military event of the early medieval period: Arab failure to take Constantinople preserved Christian Europe and allowed the Carolingian civilization to emerge.

Leo III's Iconoclasm (726 CE) — ordering the removal and destruction of religious images throughout the empire — was motivated by theological conviction (that icon veneration was idolatry) and possibly by Jewish and Islamic influence. It produced a century of violent controversy: Pope Gregory III condemned it (731), triggering Leo's seizure of papal estates in Italy; Constantine V (r. 741-775) intensified Iconoclasm, executing monks and destroying icons violently; the Second Council of Nicaea (787 CE) under Empress Irene reversed it (first Iconoclast period ended).

Empress Irene (r. 797-802 CE) — the dynasty's final ruler and history's first female Byzantine emperor — blinded and deposed her own son Constantine VI to rule alone, an act so shocking that Pope Leo III used it as justification to crown Charlemagne emperor of the Romans (800 CE), effectively splitting the Christian world. Irene was deposed in 802. The Isaurian dynasty thus both saved the Byzantine Empire and, through Iconoclasm and Irene's usurpation, catalyzed the creation of the rival Western (Carolingian) Roman Empire.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Isaurian dynasty — saving Constantinople from Arab conquest (718), triggering the Iconoclasm controversy that shaped Orthodox theology, and catalyzing Charlemagne's coronation (800) that split the Christian world — produced two of medieval history's most consequential moments: the preservation of Christian Europe and the East-West religious-political division.
